knowledgeItems.title: Why night driving needs more caution
knowledgeItems.summary: At night a driver cannot see as far ahead or around the vehicle, so anticipating potential hazards is harder.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Managing risk — Strategy 5: Driving safely at night, p.63
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: Use as general learning guidance, not as a claim that a crash will occur.

knowledgeItems.title: Speed choice after dark
knowledgeItems.summary: The handbook advises keeping speed down at night so there is more time to identify and respond to hazards.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Managing risk — Strategy 5: Driving safely at night, p.63
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: Speed must still comply with the posted limit and current road conditions.

knowledgeItems.title: Wet roads and visibility
knowledgeItems.summary: Heavy rain can reduce visibility and make roads slippery; drivers should reduce speed and, when conditions are severe, may need to stop safely and wait for improvement.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Rules and responsibilities — Safe speeds for different needs, pp.81–82
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: Do not infer current weather from historical crash records.

knowledgeItems.title: Slippery roads after rain
knowledgeItems.summary: Rain can make roads slippery, including when oil and dirt are brought to the surface; drivers should slow down and increase space from the vehicle ahead.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Rules and responsibilities — Slippery roads, p.82

knowledgeItems.title: Speed limit versus safe speed
knowledgeItems.summary: A speed-limit sign gives the maximum legal speed in good conditions; the driver still has to choose a safe speed at or below that limit for the actual conditions.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Rules and responsibilities — Speed limits / Safe speeds for different needs, pp.79–81
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: Do not use this to infer the posted limit of a specific road unless validated speed-zone data is available.

knowledgeItems.title: Speed and stopping distance
knowledgeItems.summary: Higher speed substantially increases stopping distance, reducing the time and distance available to respond to a hazard.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Rules and responsibilities — How quickly can you stop?, p.83
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: Use the handbook's examples as learning context; avoid presenting them as exact results for every vehicle/road condition.

knowledgeItems.title: Hazard perception
knowledgeItems.summary: Hazard perception means identifying possible dangers, assessing what may happen, and responding early enough to deal with the risk.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Learning to drive — Hazard perception, p.39

knowledgeItems.title: Scanning and blind spots
knowledgeItems.summary: Mirrors alone do not show every area around a vehicle; scanning and quick head checks help a driver detect hazards in blind spots when manoeuvring.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Learning to drive — Hazard perception / blind spots, pp.39–41
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: A head check should be quick; do not encourage prolonged looking away from the road ahead.

knowledgeItems.title: Minimum following-time guidance
knowledgeItems.summary: In good conditions, most drivers should leave at least a two-second gap to the vehicle in front.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Managing risk — Strategy 3: Give yourself some space, p.61
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: The handbook says 'most drivers'; do not describe two seconds as a universal fixed legal distance.

knowledgeItems.title: Increase the gap in harder conditions
knowledgeItems.summary: A larger following gap, such as three or four seconds, is presented as a safer option for young drivers and in poor visibility, darkness, wet/slippery roads, heavy loads or gravel.
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: This is safety guidance, not a fixed universal rule for every situation.

knowledgeItems.title: Traffic-light meanings
knowledgeItems.summary: Red requires stopping; yellow requires stopping unless it cannot be done safely; green permits entry only when the intersection will not be blocked.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Rules and responsibilities — Traffic controls at intersections, p.98

knowledgeItems.title: Roundabout entry
knowledgeItems.summary: When entering a roundabout, drivers must give way to vehicles already in the roundabout and to trams entering or approaching it.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Rules and responsibilities — Giving way at roundabouts, p.107

knowledgeItems.title: Regulatory versus warning signs
knowledgeItems.summary: Regulatory signs state what a road user must or must not do, while warning signs alert drivers to possible danger ahead.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Rules and responsibilities — Road signs, pp.84–90

knowledgeItems.title: Continuous dividing lines
knowledgeItems.summary: A single continuous dividing line restricts overtaking and U-turns, while limited crossing can still be permitted in specific situations described by the rules.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Rules and responsibilities — Road markings, pp.91–92
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: Preserve listed exceptions; do not simplify to 'never cross a continuous line'.

knowledgeItems.title: P-driver device restrictions
knowledgeItems.summary: Learner, P1 and P2 drivers face strict limits on touching or using portable/mounted devices while driving; navigation/audio should be set up before driving, subject to current rules.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Managing risk — Mobile phones and electronic devices, pp.53–54; P1/P2 conditions, pp.22–23
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: Rules may change; re-verify against current Victorian requirements before release.

knowledgeItems.title: Zero BAC for probationary drivers
knowledgeItems.summary: P1 and P2 probationary drivers must have zero blood alcohol concentration while driving.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Rules and responsibilities — Alcohol, p.71; P1/P2 conditions, pp.22–23

knowledgeItems.title: Late-night driving and fatigue
knowledgeItems.summary: Fatigue can impair attention, judgement and reflexes; the handbook identifies 10 pm–6 am as hours when people may normally be sleeping and advises avoiding driving when tired.
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: Do not infer that every late-night driver is fatigued; use as learning context only.

knowledgeItems.title: Sharing the road with vulnerable road users
knowledgeItems.summary: Drivers should scan for pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists, allow appropriate space, and anticipate that these road users may be less visible or more vulnerable in a collision.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Rules and responsibilities — Sharing the road, pp.125–144
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: Use current road-rule material to verify any exact passing-distance or tram-specific legal requirement.

knowledgeItems.title: Basic vehicle safety before driving
knowledgeItems.summary: Safe driving includes checking that the vehicle is roadworthy and that important safety items such as tyres, lights, windows and restraints are in suitable condition.
knowledgeItems.sourceSection: Managing risk — Vehicle safety and maintenance, pp.58–59
knowledgeItems.qualifiers: Exact legal standards should be checked against current Victorian requirements where a question depends on a numeric threshold.

questions.prompt: Why does night driving usually require more hazard awareness than daytime driving?

options.text: Because visibility ahead and around the vehicle is reduced
Because traffic always moves faster at night
Because mirrors cannot be used after dark
Because road signs stop applying after dark

questions.explanation: Reduced visibility makes it harder to see and anticipate potential hazards, so the driver needs more time and attention.

source.name: Road to Solo Driving
source.section: Strategy 5: Driving safely at night, p.63

questions.prompt: You are driving after dark and can see less of the road ahead than during the day. What is the best general response?

options.text: Rely only on the vehicle in front to identify hazards
Reduce speed as needed so you have more time to identify hazards
Keep the same speed regardless of visibility
Increase speed so the trip finishes sooner

questions.explanation: The handbook recommends keeping speed down at night because reduced visibility makes hazard anticipation harder.

Drive closer to the vehicle ahead so you can follow its lights

questions.explanation: Heavy rain can reduce visibility and grip, so speed should be reduced and severe conditions may require stopping safely until they improve.

options.text: It automatically switches off vehicle safety systems
It increases the distance needed to react and stop
It removes the driver's responsibility to scan
